cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK VI
Nausicaa at the river;\nthe naked stranger; the road to the city.
So he slept there, much-enduring noble Odysseus,\novercome with sleep and weariness. But Athena
went her way to the land and city of the Phaeacian men,\nwho once, in years past, lived in spacious Hypereia,
near the Cyclopes, men of overweening pride,\nwho kept raiding them, and were the stronger in force.
From there godlike Nausithous\nhad uprooted them and led them,
and settled them in Scheria, far from men who eat bread,\nand drove a wall around the city, and built houses,
and made temples for the gods,\nand divided out the plowlands.
But he long since had gone down to Hades, broken by fate,
and now Alcinous ruled, his counsels known from the gods.
To his house went the goddess, gray-eyed Athena,\ndevising the homecoming of great-hearted Odysseus.
She went into the richly-worked chamber where a girl\nlay sleeping, like the immortals in build and beauty:
Nausicaa, daughter of great-hearted Alcinous;\nand by her two handmaids, with beauty from the Graces,
one at each doorpost; and the shining doors were shut.
Like a breath of wind she swept to the girl's\nbed and stood above her head, and spoke to her,
in the likeness of the daughter of Dymas, famed for\nships, a girl her own age, and dear to her heart.
In her likeness gray-eyed Athena said:
"Nausicaa, how did your mother bear so careless a girl?
Your shining clothes lie there uncared-for — and your\nwedding is near, when you must wear beautiful things
yourself, and provide them for\nthose who lead you in procession:
it is from things like these that a good name goes up
among the people, and a father\nand honored mother are glad.
Come, let us go washing at the showing of dawn:
I will come with you and work\nbeside you, so you may be ready
the sooner — for truly not much longer will you be unwed:
already the best men through all the land of the\nPhaeacians are wooing you — and your own line is theirs.
Come then: press your famous father, before the dawn,\nto make ready the mules and a wagon to carry
the sashes and the robes and the shining coverlets.
And for yourself, too,\nit is far more fitting so than going
on foot: the washing-pools are a long way from the city."
So speaking, gray-eyed Athena went away to Olympus,\nwhere they say the seat of the gods stands fast
forever: not shaken by winds, never soaked by rain,\nnor does snow come near it, but clear sky
spreads cloudless there,\nand a white radiance runs over it;
in that place the blessed gods\ntake pleasure all their days.
There the gray-eyed one went,\nwhen she had counseled the girl.
At once Dawn came on her fair throne, and woke Nausicaa\nof the lovely robe; and she wondered at her dream
and went through the house to tell her parents,\nher dear father and mother. She found them within:
her mother sat at the hearth with her attendant women,\nspinning yarn dyed sea-purple; her father she met
at the door, on his way out to join the famous kings\nin council, where the lordly Phaeacians called him.
She stood close to her dear father and said:
"Papa dear, won't you make ready a wagon for me,
the high one with the good wheels,\nso I can take the fine clothes
to the river for washing, that lie about me dirty?
And for you too it is only proper,\nwhen you sit among the first men
debating counsels, to have clean clothing on your body.
And five dear sons have been born to you in these halls —\ntwo married, and three flourishing bachelors —
and they are always wanting fresh-washed clothes to wear
when they go to the dancing. All this is on my mind."
So she spoke: she was shy of naming ripe marriage\nto her dear father. But he saw it all, and answered:
"I do not grudge you the mules, child, or anything else.
Go: the slaves will make ready a wagon for you,
the high one with the good wheels,\nfitted with its top-rack."
So saying he called to the slaves, and they obeyed.
Outside, they made ready the smooth-running mule\nwagon and led the mules under and yoked them to it;
and the girl brought the shining clothing from\nher room and laid it in the polished wagon,
and her mother packed a box with heartening food\nof every kind — put in delicacies, and poured wine
in a goatskin bag; and the girl climbed up on the wagon.
And she gave her soft olive oil in a golden flask,
so she and her attendant women might\nanoint themselves after bathing.
And she took up the whip and the glossy reins
and whipped the mules to a run;\nand there was a clatter of hooves,
and they strained on without slackening,\ncarrying the clothes and her —
not alone: her handmaids went along beside her.
And when they came to the beautiful stream of the river,
where the washing-pools never fail — plenty of clear water
welling up through and running over,\nto clean the dirtiest things —
there they loosed the mules from under the\nwagon and shooed them along the eddying river
to graze the honey-sweet water-grass;\nand they lifted the clothes
from the wagon in armfuls and\ncarried them into the dark water,
and trod them briskly in the trenches, racing one another.
And when they had washed and rinsed away all the dirt,
they spread everything out in\nrows along the shingle of the sea,
where the waves washed the pebbles\ncleanest against the shore.
And when they had bathed and\nrubbed themselves richly with oil,
they took their meal by the banks of the river and\nwaited for the clothes to dry in the shining of the sun.
And when she and her slave-women\nhad had their joy of food,
they threw off their head-veils and played at ball,\nand white-armed Nausicaa led them in the singing.
As Artemis the arrow-pourer goes down the\nmountains, down long Taygetus or Erymanthus,
delighting in the boars and the running deer,\nand with her the nymphs, daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus,
play across the wild country, and Leto's heart is glad,\nfor she carries her head and brow above them all
and is known at once, though all of them are beautiful:
so the unwed girl outshone her handmaids.
But when she was about to fold the beautiful clothes,\nyoke the mules, and turn for home again,
then the goddess thought of one\nthing more, gray-eyed Athena:
that Odysseus should wake, and see the lovely-eyed girl,
and she should lead him to the city of the Phaeacian men.
So the princess tossed the ball to one of her handmaids;
the handmaid she missed, and it fell in a deep eddy,\nand they shrieked aloud. And noble Odysseus woke,
and sitting up he turned it over in his mind and heart:
"Ah me — whose country have I come to now? What men's?
Are they violent, savage, without justice,\nor kind to strangers, with hearts that fear the gods?
A female crying rang around me just now — girls' voices:
nymphs, who hold the sheer peaks of the mountains and\nthe springs of rivers and the grassy water-meadows?
Or am I now, can it be, near men with human speech?
Come — I will test it for myself, and see."
So speaking noble Odysseus slipped out from the thicket,
and from the thick wood with\nhis heavy hand he broke a branch
in leaf, to hold about his body\nand screen a man's privates.
And he went like a mountain-bred lion, sure of his strength,\nwho goes on through rain and wind, his two eyes
burning, and he comes down on the cattle or the\nsheep or the wild deer, for his belly commands him
to make trial of the flocks —\neven to enter the close-built fold:
so Odysseus was about to come among the fair-braided\ngirls, naked as he was: for need had come upon him.
And he loomed terrible before them,\ncrusted with the salt sea's brine,
and they scattered, one here,\none there, along the jutting sandspits.
Alone the daughter of Alcinous stayed: for Athena
set courage in her heart and took\nthe trembling from her limbs.
She stood and faced him, holding\nher ground. And Odysseus weighed it,
whether to clasp the knees of the lovely-eyed girl and beg,\nor standing apart as he was, with honeyed words,
to beg her to show him the city and give him clothing.
And as he weighed it, this seemed the better way:
to stand apart and beg with honeyed words,\nlest the girl's heart take anger if he touched her knees.
At once he spoke — a honeyed speech, and a shrewd one:
"I am at your knees, queen — goddess or mortal, are you?
If you are one of the gods who hold wide heaven,\nthen it is to Artemis, daughter of great Zeus,
that I liken you nearest —\nin beauty, in stature, in bearing.
But if you are one of the mortals who live on the earth,
three times blessed your father and your honored mother,
three times blessed your brothers! Surely their hearts
are warmed through with gladness always because of you,
watching such a young shoot go stepping into the dance.
But blessed at heart above all others is that man
who weighs down the scales of the\nbride-gifts and leads you home.
For my eyes have never seen a mortal like you,\nnot man, not woman. Awe takes me, looking at you.
In Delos once, beside Apollo's altar, I saw such a thing:\nthe young shoot of a date-palm springing up —
for I came there too, and a great host followed me,\non that road where my bitter cares were to be —
and just as, seeing that, I stood amazed at heart
a long time, since no such stem\nhad ever risen from the earth,
so, lady, I wonder at you, amazed, and I am terribly\nafraid to touch your knees. But hard grief is upon me.
Yesterday, on the twentieth day,\nI escaped the wine-dark sea:
all that time the waves carried me,\nand the driving storms,
away from the island Ogygia.\nAnd now some power has cast me here —
to suffer some new evil in this place too,\nno doubt: for I do not think
the evil will stop; the gods will\naccomplish plenty more first.
But pity me, queen. After many hard labors it\nis to you first I have come; I know not one
of the others whose city and land this is.
Show me the town, and give me a rag to throw around me —
if perhaps you had some wrapping-cloth\nfor the linen when you came.
And may the gods grant you all your heart desires:
a husband and a house — and may they add like-mindedness,
the good kind. For nothing is\nstronger or better than that:
when two who think alike keep house together,\na man and his wife — much grief to their ill-wishers,
joy to their friends; and they themselves know it best."
Then white-armed Nausicaa answered him:
"Stranger — since you seem\nneither base nor witless a man —
it is Olympian Zeus himself who deals out fortune to\nmankind, to good and bad, to each one as he wills;
and to you, I suppose, he gave this lot,\nand you must bear it, come what may.
But now, since you have come to our city and our land,
you shall not want for clothing, nor for anything\nelse that is owed a hard-worn suppliant when he comes.
I will show you the town,\nand tell you the name of the people.
The Phaeacians hold this city and this land,\nand I am the daughter of great-hearted Alcinous,
on whom the strength and power of the Phaeacians hang."
She spoke, and called to her fair-braided handmaids:
"Stand still, you girls! Where are\nyou running at the sight of a man?
You cannot think he is one of an enemy people?
There is no living mortal, and there will be none,\nwho could come bearing war into the land
of the Phaeacian men. For we are\nvery dear to the deathless ones,
and we live apart, in the much-surging sea,\nat the world's edge, and no other mortals mix with us.
No — this is some poor wanderer come here astray,
whom we must care for now.\nFrom Zeus they come, all of them,
strangers and beggars; and a gift, though small, is dear.
Come, girls: give the stranger food and drink,
and bathe him in the river,\nwhere there is shelter from the wind."
So she spoke; and they stood, and called to one another,
and they set Odysseus down in the\nsheltered place, as she commanded —
Nausicaa, daughter of great-hearted Alcinous —\nand laid a mantle and a tunic by him for clothing,
and gave him soft olive oil in the golden flask,\nand urged him to bathe in the streams of the river.
Then noble Odysseus spoke among the handmaids:
"Stand off there, girls, at a distance, so that I myself
may wash the brine from my shoulders, and rub myself
with oil: it is long indeed since oil came near my skin.
But I will not bathe in front of you. I would be\nashamed to stand naked among fair-braided girls."
So he spoke; and they went apart, and told the girl.
And noble Odysseus washed his body in the river,
sluicing off the brine that caked\nhis back and broad shoulders,
and scrubbed from his head the\nsalt-scurf of the barren sea.
And when he had washed all over,\nand rubbed himself with oil,
and put on the clothes the unwed girl had given him,\nthen Athena, born of Zeus, made him
taller to look at, and broader, and down from his head
she made the locks flow in curls,\nlike the hyacinth flower.
As when a man lays gold over silver — a craftsman\nwhom Hephaestus and Pallas Athena have taught
art of every kind, and he finishes works full of grace —\nso she poured grace over his head and shoulders.
Then he went apart and sat on the shingle of the sea,
shining with beauty and grace. And the girl gazed at him,\nand spoke among her fair-braided handmaids:
"Listen, my white-armed girls, while I say something.
Not against the will of all the gods who hold Olympus\ndoes this man come among the godlike Phaeacians.
Before, I confess, he seemed to me a sorry sight;\nnow he is like the gods who hold wide heaven.
If only such a man might be called my husband,\nliving here — if only it pleased him to stay!
But come, girls: give the stranger food and drink."
So she spoke, and they listened well and obeyed,\nand set food and drink beside Odysseus.
And he drank and ate, much-enduring noble Odysseus,\nravenously: it was long since he had tasted food.
But white-armed Nausicaa thought of one thing more:
she folded the clothes and stowed\nthem in the beautiful wagon,
and yoked the strong-hoofed mules, and mounted herself,
and called Odysseus on, and spoke a word, and named him:
"Up now, stranger, and we go\nto the city, so I may send you
to the house of my wise father — where, I promise you,\nyou will meet the best men of all the Phaeacians.
Only do exactly this —\nyou do not seem to me short of sense.
While we are passing the fields and the works of men,\nwalk with the handmaids, behind the mules and wagon,
briskly; I will lead the way.
But when we are about to enter\nthe city — a high wall rings it,
and a beautiful harbor lies on either side of the town,
with a narrow causeway in;\nand the curved ships are drawn up
along the road, for every man has his own slip there;
and there is the gathering-place\naround Poseidon's fine precinct,
fitted with quarried stones set deep in the earth;\nand there men see to the tackle of their black ships,
the cables and the sails, and fine down their oars —
for the Phaeacians care nothing for the bow or the quiver,
but for masts, and ships' oars,\nand the trim ships themselves,
in which they delight as they cross the gray salt sea —
it is their ugly talk I shrink from:\nsomeone behind my back
There are insolent men enough in the town;\nand one of the meaner sort, meeting us, might say:
'Who is this following Nausicaa — this tall handsome
stranger? Where did she find him?\nA husband for her, no doubt!
Some castaway she has taken up, off his ship,\na man from far parts — since nobody lives near us;
or some god, long prayed-for, come down to her out of\nheaven in answer, and hers he will be all her days!
Better so, if she has gone out and found herself a husband
from elsewhere — since she\nscorns her own, here in the land,
the Phaeacians, though many fine men are wooing her!'
So they will say, and it would be a reproach against me.
And I would blame another girl who did such things myself:
who, against the will of her\ndear father and mother living,
kept company with men before the day of open marriage.
So, stranger, mark my word quickly, and you will\nwin escort and homecoming from my father soonest.
You will find a shining grove of Athena near the road —
poplars; a spring wells up in it; a meadow lies around it.
There is my father's park there, and his flourishing orchard,\nas far from the city as a man's shout carries.
Sit down there and wait a while, until we have\nentered the town and reached my father's house.
But when you judge that we have reached the house,\nthen go into the city of the Phaeacians, and ask
for the house of my father, great-hearted Alcinous.
It is easily known: a little child could lead you —\na baby; for the houses of the Phaeacians are not built
anything like it — such is the house of the hero
Alcinous. And once the buildings\nand the court have hidden you,
go quickly straight through the great hall, until you come
to my mother. She sits at the\nhearth in the light of the fire,
spinning yarn dyed sea-purple — a wonder to see —
leaning against a pillar,\nand her slave-women sit behind her.
And there my father's chair is tilted close to hers,\nwhere he sits and drinks his wine like an immortal.
Pass him by, and throw your arms around the knees of\nmy mother — if you would see your day of homecoming
with rejoicing, and quickly,\nthough you come from very far.
If she once takes kindly thought for you in her heart,
then there is hope you will see your own people,\nand come to your well-built house and your own fatherland."
So speaking she touched the mules with the shining whip,\nand they quickly left the flowing river behind.
Well they trotted, well they wheeled their legs along,
and she drove with care,\nso that the walkers could keep pace —
the handmaids and Odysseus —\nand used the lash with judgment.
And the sun went down, and they came to the famous\ngrove sacred to Athena. There noble Odysseus sat down,
and at once he prayed to the daughter of great Zeus:
"Hear me, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, Unwearied One.
Hear me now at last, since before you never heard me
when I was broken — when the famous earth-shaker broke me.
Grant that I come among the\nPhaeacians pitied, and a friend."
So he spoke in prayer, and Pallas Athena heard him.
But she did not yet show herself\nto him face to face: she stood
in awe of her father's brother, who raged on furiously
against godlike Odysseus,\nuntil the day he reached his own land.
